D1 research authoring, batch 83 (2026-09-27): ONE ASSOCIATION_ONLY draft mapping added at rank 1 (stress-fractures) pending qualified-human citation verification under docs/citation-verification-sop.md; mapping approval is not citation verification. This edge is deliberately the WEAKEST in batch 83 and is registered as a shared-overload and differential-overlap association rather than as a causal route. No located anchor reports calcaneal apophysitis and calcaneal stress fracture co-occurring in the same patient, or occurring in sequence; the three anchors characterise altered loading and mechanism, not the two conditions together.

Classification guard: the single edge asserts association only (etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, hypothesizedOnly:true) at BIOMECHANICAL_ALTERATION, chosen to name the SHARED LOADING pathway rather than a lesion progression. Its causation status states that a calcaneal stress fracture is a fatigue injury of the posterior calcaneus typically in the adolescent whereas Sever's disease is a traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis at a different skeletal site and age, so a causal reading is anatomically implausible as stated, and that any stress-fracture claim must rest on an independent imaging-documented fracture diagnosis rather than on the apophysitis label.

Withheld routes and duplicate-scope screen: no avulsion-fracture edge (MISSING IDENTITY - the documented rare complication of calcaneal apophysitis is an avulsion fracture of the apophysis and the catalog carries no avulsion-fracture identity); no post-traumatic-osteoarthritis and no malunion-nonunion-of-fractures edge (EVIDENCE-INSUFFICIENT, neither reported by the located anchors); no plantar-fasciitis edge (MISSING IDENTITY, and it is a differential-diagnostic consideration rather than an associated condition); no attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder edge (MISSING IDENTITY, though a prospective observational study of a possible association was located in the search and is recorded here as a named candidate for a future batch); and no attention-deficit or developmental edge for the same identity reason. A conservative-management treatment-efficacy review was located and reviewed but not registered because it addresses treatment rather than any secondary-condition relationship.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Sever's disease and calcaneal stress fracture share an overuse mechanism and a documented differential-diagnostic problem in the same anatomical site, and the located evidence characterises the altered loading that underlies both: a review of clinical, pathologic, and therapeutic considerations for Sever's disease of the pediatric population sets out the traction-apophysitis mechanism at the calcaneal apophysis in physically active children (PMID 34531270); a gait study of vertical ground reaction forces in children with and without calcaneal apophysitis documents altered lower-limb loading during gait in the affected group (PMID 31054494); and a case-control study reports that slow velocity of the centre of pressure and high heel pressures may increase the risk of Sever's disease, directly linking plantar loading to the condition (PMID 30453930); recorded as a shared-overload and differential-overlap association only, and this is the weakest edge in batch 83 by design, with the located evidence establishing altered biomechanics and a differential relationship but NOT establishing that apophysitis causes a stress fracture.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: This edge asserts materially less than its name suggests and the causation status says so in terms: the located evidence supports a SHARED OVERUSE MECHANISM and a DIFFERENTIAL-DIAGNOSTIC OVERLAP between calcaneal apophysitis and calcaneal stress fracture in the active child, and it does NOT support a claim that one produces the other. A calcaneal stress fracture is a fatigue injury of the posterior calcaneus, typically in the adolescent, whereas Sever's disease is a traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis at a different skeletal site and age, so a causal reading is anatomically implausible as stated and this edge is registered as an association of mechanism rather than a progression. Critically, the located evidence assembled for this file contains NO anchor reporting the two conditions co-occurring in the same patient, NO anchor reporting a stress fracture developing after a documented apophysitis, and NO anchor quantifying how often the two are confused, so no rate may be quoted and none is quoted. The anchors are a narrative review, a gait biomechanics study, and a case-control study of plantar pressure, none of which is a study of the two conditions together. Individual claims require a dated Sever's disease diagnosis and, if a stress fracture is separately claimed, an independent imaging-documented fracture diagnosis, since the two conditions share a site and an age group and are routinely considered together.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is repetitive mechanical overload of the plantar surface transmitted through the calcaneus, in which high heel pressures and slow centre-of-pressure velocity increase traction at the calcaneal apophysis and in adolescent bone raise fatigue loading of the posterior calcaneus, so that the SAME altered loading that produces traction apophysitis at the apophysis is the loading that would produce a fatigue fracture at the calcaneal body; the vector is named as a shared loading pathway rather than a causal progression precisely because the located evidence documents the loading, not the progression from one lesion to the other.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at narrative-review, gait-biomechanics, and case-control class, and registered as this file's SOLE edge at explicitly the lowest evidential strength in batch 83, which the conservative standard records on the face of the edge rather than smoothing over: the clinical review supplies the traction-apophysitis mechanism and the pediatric context (PMID 34531270); the gait study supplies quantified altered vertical ground reaction force in affected children (PMID 31054494); and the case-control study supplies the direct plantar-loading link, reporting slow centre-of-pressure velocity and high heel pressures as risk factors (PMID 30453930). Because the three anchors characterise mechanism and load but never report the two conditions together, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only, frames it explicitly as shared-overload and differential overlap, and requires that any stress-fracture claim rest on an independent imaging-documented fracture diagnosis rather than on the apophysitis label.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: This is the weakest edge in batch 83 and its evidence gaps are correspondingly explicit: NO located anchor reports calcaneal apophysitis and calcaneal stress fracture co-occurring in the same patient; NO anchor reports a stress fracture developing after a documented apophysitis; NO anchor quantifies diagnostic confusion between the two, which is the practical problem a clinician faces; NO anchor supplies a non-apophysitis comparison group for any stress-fracture outcome; and NO anchor is a study of the two conditions together at all. The three anchors are a narrative review, a gait biomechanics comparison, and a case-control study of plantar pressure, and a treatment-efficacy review was located and reviewed but not registered because it addresses conservative management rather than the stress-fracture relationship. The avulsion-fracture route was reviewed and withheld as MISSING IDENTITY, since the documented rare complication of calcaneal apophysitis is an avulsion fracture of the apophysis and the catalog carries no avulsion-fracture identity, and the post-traumatic-osteoarthritis and malunion-nonunion routes were withheld as EVIDENCE-INSUFFICIENT.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Calcaneal stress fracture arising from the same overuse mechanism but at a different skeletal site and typically a different age, which must be independently imaged rather than inferred from the apophysitis diagnosis
Avulsion fracture of the calcaneal apophysis, the documented rare complication of the condition, which requires independent imaging
Plantar fasciitis and other causes of pediatric heel pain sharing the presentation but not the mechanism
Achilles tendinopathy or enthesopathy, which the located case literature reports in association with calcaneal apophysitis

suggestions.rationale: Authoring registers this edge as a deliberately weak, mechanistically-framed candidate rather than a strong claim, because the catalog carries no better-identified target for this condition and because the located evidence does document a shared overuse loading pathway in the same anatomic site with a genuine differential-diagnostic problem. The conservative framing states outright that no located anchor reports the two conditions co-occurring or occurring in sequence, classifies the edge as BIOMECHANICAL_ALTERATION to name the shared loading rather than a lesion progression, and requires an independent imaging-documented fracture diagnosis for any stress-fracture claim.

Anchors are the review of the clinical, pathologic, and therapeutic considerations of Sever's disease in the pediatric population (PMID 34531270), the gait study comparing vertical ground reaction forces in children with and without calcaneal apophysitis (PMID 31054494), and the case-control study reporting that slow centre-of-pressure velocity and high heel pressures increase risk (PMID 30453930).
